extracted.intended_audience: readers of satirical Renaissance literature / general literary audience (students and scholars of Rabelais)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the normative principles and practices (presented satirically) that Bridlegoose and other judicial officers follow when deciding suits, reconciling parties, and administering justice. Focuses on procedural, moral, and pragmatic maxims the text gives for judging and reconciling disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfections of nature excuse judicial errors
rubrics_metrics.description: "the imperfections of nature should never be imputed unto any for crimes and transgressions; as appeareth..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridlegoose asks the court to consider his failing sight and cites canonical authority that natural infirmities (age, dimmed sight) should not be charged as moral culpability for mistaken judgments; used as an exculpatory ground for judicial mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Alea Judiciorum (deciding by the dice) is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: "The dice, quoth Bridlegoose, of sentences at law, decrees, and peremptory judgments, Alea Judiciorum... Mark, that chance and fortune are good, honest, profitable, and necessary for ending of and putting a final closure to dissensions and debates in suits at law."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents resorting to chance as a recognized (even canonically supported) method to terminate disputes; citations to glosses and jurists are offered to legitimize aleatory decision-making when used according to custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to customary practice and other judges
rubrics_metrics.description: "My practice is therein the same with that of your other worships, and as the custom of the judicatory requires..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures should follow established judicial custom and the practice of one's peers; Bridlegoose repeatedly invokes glosses and authorities to justify doing 'as your other worships do'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalities and documentary completeness are necessary — omission voids proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: "First, for formality sake, the omission whereof, that it maketh all, whatever is done, to be of no force nor value..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long laundry-list of pleadings, instruments, and documents is cited to show the necessity of procedural formalities: their presence gives validity; their omission can void outcomes. Documents also serve ritual and practical purposes beyond substantive fact-finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small dice in obscure/many-bag cases; large dice when matters are plain
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have other large great dice... which I employ... when the matter is more plain, clear, and liquid... But when there are many bags on the one side and on the other, I then use my little small dice... Semper in obscuris quod minimum est sequimur."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A procedural rule for which instrument of chance to use: in obscure or complex cases (many pleadings/bags) use the 'small' dice; in clear/simple cases use the 'large' dice. Supported by cited legal maxim about following the least in obscurities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness in order of hazard: defendant first
rubrics_metrics.description: "I posit on the end of a table in my closet all the pokes and bags of the defendant, and then allow unto him the first hazard of the dice... Then do I likewise... throw the dice for [the plaintiff], and forthwith livre him his chance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific procedural sequencing: defendant's bags are placed and the defendant is given the first throw; plaintiff follows. Framed as conforming to judicial custom and visibility ('visum visu') principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and protraction of judgment until the case 'ripens'
rubrics_metrics.description: "time ripeneth and bringeth all things to maturity... I defer, protract, delay, prolong... the time of giving a definitive sentence, to the end that the suit... may... come at last to its full ripeness and maturity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifies postponement with metaphors (medicine, harvest): delay allows truth to emerge, parties to cool, and the matter to mature; protraction is defended by legal authorities and analogies to natural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow recreation/exercise to preserve officers' health
rubrics_metrics.description: "they are useful and steadable to me... in lieu of some other honest and healthful exercise. The late Master Othoman Vadet... hath frequently told me that the lack and default of bodily exercise is the chief... cause of the little health and short lives of all officers of justice..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits games and physical pastimes (e.g., muss) for judges and officers as salutary; such recreation is defended by medical authority and legal commentators and is therefore excusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation of procedural acts and papers gives a suit form and legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: "But when there are heaps of these legiformal papers packed, piled... then is it that with a good reason we may term that suit... well-formed and fashioned..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text portrays the growth of a suit as a process of generating documents/acts; the presence of many formal acts (hearings, warrants, reports) confers shape, gravity, and legitimacy to an initially shapeless action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritualized pauses (e.g., requiring plaintiff to sleep) as formal steps in process
rubrics_metrics.description: "First, I permit the plaintiff to depart from the court, enjoining him not to presume to return thither till he preallably should have taken a good sound and profound sleep, which is to serve for the prime entry and introduction to the legal carrying on of the business. In the next place, a formal report is to be made to me of his having slept."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes quasi-ceremonial requirements (sleep and attestation) before proceeding in criminal matters; presented as formalistic devices that generate further procedural acts and thereby build the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediator strategy: reconcile parties when they are exhausted or out of money
rubrics_metrics.description: "I would take them at that very instant nick of time when both those of the one and the other side should be weary and tired of making war, when they had voided and emptied their own cashes and coffers... there I am sure... they should be forced to have a little respite..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel for peacemaking: pick the moment when disputants are financially drained or fatigued—then they are likelier to accept reconciliation. Illustrated with the father/son Dandin story about timing and appetite for accords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediator should create a social act of reconciliation (drink together) as sign of covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: "he straight made the parties agreed and pacified to drink together as a sure and infallible token and symbol of a perfect and completely well-cemented reconciliation"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recommended method for sealing an accord: convert settlement into a convivial social act (drinking together) to symbolize and cement reconciliation; presented as tried custom with social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration for pardon: old age, simplicity, and long upright record
rubrics_metrics.description: "I observe, gentlemen, in this Bridlegoose several things which induce me to represent before you that it is my opinion he should be pardoned. In the first place, his old age; secondly, his simplicity... this one, sole, and single fault of his ought to be quite forgotten... by that immense... ocean of just dooms and sentences which heretofore he hath given..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable grounds for mercy are offered: advanced age, simplicity, and a long history of acceptable judgments weigh in favour of pardon; use of metaphor (drop in the river) to argue the insignificance of one fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardon conditional on restitution/surety to the injured party
rubrics_metrics.description: "First, that he satisfy, or put a sufficient surety for the satisfaction of the party wronged by the injustice of the sentence in question."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel (speaking for mercy) imposes remedial condition(s): the accused judge must make amends or provide security for satisfaction of the harmed party as a precondition of pardon (first condition stated; more to follow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize certain games (muss) as lawful and excusable for judges
rubrics_metrics.description: "the game of the muss is honest, healthful, ancient, and lawful... Such as play and sport it at the muss are excusable in and by law"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly names a particular pastime as lawful recreation for judicial officers; used to justify jocular/extraneous behaviour in judicial settings.
